tests/static/test_event_type_coverage.py — PATCH-D: the drift guard.

PATCH-A introduced relay/emitter.py's EventType enum as the single
source of truth for event types, and PATCH-B repointed eo/notify.py's
VALID_KINDS at a curated subset of it (NOTIFY_KINDS), closing the two
places this codebase's event-type allowlist used to drift out of sync
with its own call sites. PATCH-C made an unrecognized type degrade
(logged + skipped) instead of raising, so that drift can no longer
crash a task run in production.

None of that stops drift from *happening* again -- it just stops it
from being catastrophic when it does. A call site can still pass a
plain string literal (nothing enforces "always use EventType.X"), and
if that literal is never added to EventType, the event just silently
never gets sent -- which is much better than crashing the run, but is
still a real, findable bug that's better caught at CI time than
discovered later by "huh, why did this notification/diagram/deploy
status never show up on the frontend."

This file is that catch: it statically walks every .py file under
agents/, eo/, and relay/ and asserts every string literal passed as an
event_type / kind argument to emit_event(), emit_user_event(), or
notify() resolves to a real EventType / NOTIFY_KINDS member. It does
NOT flag calls that already pass EventType.X directly (an Attribute
node, not a string Constant) -- those are already statically safe:
a typo there is an AttributeError at import time, long before th

S04b: the device socket's runtime needs are provided by every deployment path.

backend/codeagent/ws.py validates every message with protocol/validate.py, which needs

  * jsonschema (with `referencing`, `jsonschema-specifications` and `rpds-py`), and
  * the protocol/ directory itself (protocol/v1/*.json), found by
    codeagent.ws.load_protocol() at <backend>/protocol or <repo root>/protocol.

Without either, load_protocol() raises ProtocolUnavailable and the socket fails closed
(`internal`, close 1011) -- safe, but the feature would be dead on arrival in a container.
This file reads the deployment files as TEXT, so it holds where Docker and pip are not
available, and fails on exactly the three ways that regression can come back:

  1. the pins the two requirements files share drift apart (protocol/requirements.txt is
     what the `protocol` CI job installs, backend/requirements.txt is what ships; a
     version that differs between them means the contract is tested against one
     jsonschema and served by another);
  2. backend.Dockerfile stops copying protocol/ to /app/protocol (the image's layout:
     WORKDIR /app holds backend/, so <backend>/protocol is /app/protocol);
  3. docker-compose.dev.yml stops mounting ./protocol at /app/protocol (its
     `./backend:/app` bind mount hides everything the image copied under /app, so the
     directory has to be mounted back in; read-only because nothing writes there).

That load_protocol() really succeeds in a backend install

S06 migration 0014: invariants checked on the SQL text itself, so they hold even
where no database is available (CI). The real-Postgres behaviour of the same
properties is in tests/integration/test_runs_pg.py.

  * THE RULE THIS FILE EXISTS FOR (build plan O1 / 11.4): the `runs` table has no
    content column. Checked three ways: the column list is an allow-list (adding a
    column means editing this test on purpose), no column name can carry content, and
    every text column is either an id or bounded by a CHECK that makes it a vocabulary
    word, a code or an enumeration -- never free text. No json / bytea / array column.
  * RLS enabled AND forced; policies dropped before they are created;
  * grants live in the same file, are table-level, go only to minime_app, and nothing
    grants DELETE; B01's replay of ALL migrations still works with 0014 present and
    derives {select, insert, update} for runs;
  * what the grants cannot express is carried by a BEFORE UPDATE trigger written as a
    plain CREATE FUNCTION whose messages never print a row value;
  * the CHECKs agree with codeagent/runs.py and with protocol/v1 (state list, run id
    pattern, terminal states);
  * the file is safe to paste into the Supabase SQL editor.

It also holds the structural logging check for codeagent/runs.py (the S04 test only
scans ws.py and connections.py): no logging call may name a content-carrying variable,
ask for a traceback or log an exception object.

B01 (M2C Phase 0): the SQL in the code-file store versus the grants in the migrations.

WHY THIS TEST EXISTS. The app connects as the low-privilege `minime_app` role
(migration 0003), and later migrations narrow what that role may do to
individual tables. Migration 0009 grants `SELECT, INSERT, DELETE` on
workspace_code_file_versions and then REVOKEs UPDATE, on purpose: a version row
is a fact about the past and is never rewritten. move_path() once ran
`UPDATE workspace_code_file_versions SET file_path = ...`; Postgres answered
"permission denied" and every move or rename in the Build tab returned a 500.
The unit tests use a fake cursor, so no grant was ever consulted and nothing
caught it. tests/integration/test_workspace_code_files_pg.py now catches it
against a real database, but only when someone points MINIME_TEST_DATABASE_URL
at one. THIS test needs no database: it reads the migrations, works out what
`minime_app` can do to each table, reads the SQL out of the Python module, and
fails when the two disagree. It runs in the default `pytest tests/static` run.

HOW IT WORKS (three small parts, all standard library).

  1. GrantLedger replays backend/migrations/*.sql in filename order and keeps
     the NET privileges `minime_app` holds on each table: a GRANT adds, a
     REVOKE removes, order matters (0003 grants UPDATE+DELETE on audit_log and
     revokes them again in the same file), and grants to PUBLIC count too
     because `minime_app` inherits them. Comments, quoted s

S01 call-site inventory: every caller of generate_text() / stream_completion()
and how its usage is attributed in the shared ledger.

WHY THIS TEST EXISTS. The ledger hook in utils/llm_client.py meters every real
call, but WHO the call is billed to comes from eo/usage_context.py, which only
knows what an entry point told it. A new LLM caller reached from a new,
un-scoped entry point silently meters as 'system' -- usage nobody is charged
for. This test pins the full list so adding a caller forces a decision here.

If it fails because you added or moved a caller: add the file below with the
right category, and if the caller is reachable from a route or job that does
not open a usage scope, either open one (usage_context.attributed / scope) or
mark it SYSTEM on purpose. Keep docs/usage-ledger-call-sites.md in step.

Categories:
  TASK      reached only through api/task_runner.py's run_task / preview_task /
            confirm_task / run_task_from_template (decorated with
            usage_context.attributed) or POST /api/resume (scoped in the route)
            -> attributed to the task's owner, surface 'web'.
  NOTEBOOK  reached through the notebook routes that take owner_id and are
            decorated with usage_context.attributed -> owner, surface 'web'.
  SYSTEM    attributed to surface 'system' (user_id NULL). Either deliberate
            (platform-initiated work) or a KNOWN GAP (a user-initiated route
            that has no owner in scope yet) -- see the notes.
  UNUSE
